To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a small series of 2′-modified uracil nucleoside phosphonic acid analogues were synthesized and evaluated for antiviral activity; and 2) anomerization of the uracil nucleotide phosphonic acid analogs was observed during the deprotection of the protecting groups.
5-(hetro)arylated nucleoside phosphates have a broad antiviral activity, and that the anomeric form of the 5-(heto)arylated nucleotide has a strong influence on the biological activity.

5-substituents of uridine phosphonates have a significant impact on the antiviral activity of these nucleotide analogues, and that the 5-arylated nucleoside phosphates can be synthesized by the Wittig reaction followed by Suzuki–Miyura coupling and subsequent deprotection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and synthesis of nucleoside phosphonic acid derivatives and the evaluation of their biological activity.
the development of new antiviral agents and with the elucidation of structure–activity relationships of nucleoside analogues.
the synthesis and antiviral activity of 5-aryl-modified nucleotide phosphonate derivatives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
5-phenyl-2′-deoxynucleoside analogues are not promising as antiviral agents.
5-aryl-modified nucleotide analogues have no or little antiviral activity.
the antiviral activity of the 5-modified uridine phosphonates is not only dependent on the substitution at position 5 but also on the configuration of the anomeric carbon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
5-(hetro)aryl-modified 2′- deoxyuridine phosphonate analogues are not suitable for antiviral drug development.
2′- deoxy-5-(heterocycles)uridyl phosphonates are potent inhibitors of the replication of several RNA viruses, with EC _{50} values ranging from 0.5 to 5 μM.

The main takeaway from our work is that

5-substitution of 2′- deoxyuridine- 5′-phosphate is not tolerated by the vast majority of the viruses tested, with the exception of a few cases of weak activity against herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).

5-phenyl-modified uridine phosphonates display antiviral activity, with a particular focus on the 5-phenylethyne derivative, which was found to be active against a broad panel including herpes simplex virus type 1, herpes simplex virus type-2 and cytomegalovirus.
the anomeric configuration of the phosphonate is not crucial to antiviral activity, but rather the nature of the 5-aryl substituent.
